newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa fears worst as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa fears worst as rebels advance.

text.p: Fear and apprehension gripped Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Tuesday after embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko returned to the city in defiance of rebel demands that he quit.
With Laurent Kabila's rebels reported less than 85 km (50 miles) from the usually teeming capital of five million people, residents were slow to venture out, cautiously checking the streets.

"I looked out this morning at 6 a.m. and there was nobody in my street. That was highly unusual," said a hotel attendant who lives in the suburbs. A regular church goer, he found few worshippers when he arrived for early morning mass.
Mobutu, who has dominated the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa since seizing power in 1965, returned to the city on Monday after failed peace talks.
Aides said the veteran leader, who is battling cancer as well as the whirlwind rebel advance, was resting in his presidential villa in Kinshasa's heavily guarded Tshatshi military camp.
In the city centre commercial district scores of people, hungry for the latest news, clustered around newspaper vendors -- avidly reading newspapers spread out on the ground.
Many Kinshasa residents openly welcome the prospect of Kabila's arrival but fear the response of Mobutu's soldiers, who in the past have looted and pillaged before fleeing the advancing rebels.

Markets operated normally and traffic picked up as the morning wore on but, with Mobutu showing signs of hardening his position, newspapers predicted the imminent arrival of Kabila. Some hinted at difficult times if Mobutu opted to fight.
"Kabila is preparing his best men for the job of evicting Mobutu," the opposition newspaper La Tempete announced.

"Washington prepares Kabila's entry into Kinshasa," Le Potentiel newspaper headlined, focusing on comments from U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson that Washington wanted a "soft landing" when the rebels arrived.
Mobutu's foreign minister, Kamanda wa Kamanda, on Monday dismissed reports Mobutu had written to U.S. President Bill Clinton pledging to resign.
A communique issued after weekend talks between Mobutu, Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mendela on a South African ship in Congo said Mobutu had offered to hand over to an elected successor.
Kamanda, who advised Mobutu during the talks, said on Monday Mobutu was willing to do this if he decided it was inopportune to stand in elections himself.
Anonymous pamphlets distributed in the city on Monday urged support for the rebels and called on the people of the capital to wear white scarves as a sign of solidarity with them.
With Mobutu and his feared presidential guard still in the city, white scarves, once commonplace in the city, were notable by their absence on Tuesday.
